title: An anarchist's lit bomb lands next to Keaton; he calmly picks it up and lights his cigarette off the fuse
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: Total unbothered calm while holding the thing that is about to ruin everything: perfect 'it's fine' energy.

title: Keaton's furniture wagon rolls past a line of marching police and the whole frame erupts into a white explosion
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: Orderly parade to total white-out in one beat: the universal 'and then it all blew up' cut-away.

title: Keaton stumbles in the street as an entire city's police force floods toward the camera
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: A wall of cops charging straight at the lens reads instantly as 'run'.

title: Keaton on his wagon tips his straw hat to the crowd, sure the parade cheers are for him
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: Gracious little hat-tip of a man who has no idea what's coming: pure overconfidence.

title: Keaton, seated on the wagon, slowly looks back over his shoulder at the chaos behind him, then faces front stone-faced
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: The 'did I do that? ...anyway' look-back, then eyes front as if nothing happened.

title: Keaton sits slumped on the wagon with his chin propped in his hand, bored and defeated
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: Classic waiting-forever slouch with the Great Stone Face.

title: Keaton thumbs through a wad of bills and reluctantly peels one off to pay the cabbie
film: Cops (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1922)
why: Careful bill-counting and a grudging hand-over: instant 'paying for it' cut.

title: Keaton sits on a bench and holds a long, blank, sideways deadpan stare
why: The signature Great Stone Face: says 'I have nothing to add' louder than any line.

title: Close-up of a pencil turning a $1.00 price tag into $4.00
why: Visible markup gag: perfect after any line about prices, inflation or 'trust me it was expensive'.

title: On a parlor couch next to his sweetheart, Keaton glances at her, loses his nerve and stares innocently at the ceiling
why: Two people, zero idea what to do: the awkward-silence head tilt says it all.

title: The projectionist Keaton props his head on his hand and slowly nods off beside the projector
why: Everyone's 'meeting that could have been an email' face.

title: Keaton grabs a water-tower spout and the full torrent dumps him onto the tracks
why: A man swallowed by a waterfall: the cleanest 'that went badly' cut-away.

title: Keaton rides the handlebars of a driverless motorcycle, arms akimbo and serene, as traffic whips past
why: Supreme confidence with no one steering: the face of 'everything is under control'.

title: Keaton, still on the runaway handlebars, clutches his head as a locomotive thunders past inches away
why: Instinctive head-clutch as disaster roars by: the 'I can't look' reaction.

title: Projectionist Keaton watches the movie screen, glances at his girl and scratches his head, puzzled
why: The famous closing head-scratch: universal 'wait, how does that work?'.

title: The burly father sits back, throws up his fists and roars with laughter
film: Neighbors (Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline, 1920)
why: Big, fist-pumping cackle: an instant 'lmao' cut.

title: Chaplin swings open a giant bank vault with a grand flourish, then plants his hands on his hips, very pleased with himself
why: Pure unearned confidence: the pose of someone sure they have it all under control

title: Chaplin secretly slips a lucky horseshoe into his boxing glove, darting sly glances to make sure nobody is watching
why: The face of someone who just found a loophole and knows it

title: A mustached villain's eye appears in a knothole in the fence and darts suspiciously side to side
why: A giant rolling eyeball in a hole is instant 'I see what you are doing'

title: Eric Campbell, huge and mustached, slowly turns and glowers with bulging, furious eyes
why: An enormous cartoon-villain glare that reads instantly as 'excuse me?'

title: A dapper old gentleman with a mustache goggles in wide-eyed astonishment
why: Pure bug-eyed disbelief in a tight close-up, no context needed

title: A society lady lifts her chin, closes her eyes and turns her head away in lofty disdain
why: The universal 'I'm not even dignifying that with a response'

title: Chaplin glides in on roller skates, collides with a man and both crash to the floor with skates in the air
why: Smooth confidence to legs-in-the-air wipeout in three seconds

title: A gymnast whirls upside-down around a bar and crashes face-first to the floor while Chaplin stands by unbothered
why: Big athletic flourish, immediate humiliating faceplant

title: A bank clerk counting a pile of cash is startled and flings the bills into the air, throwing up his hands
why: Money literally flying away: perfect for any expense or price reveal

title: Chaplin, hand clamped over his mouth, turns slowly to face the camera with anxious, worried eyes
why: The silent 'oh no, what have I done' as he slowly turns to the lens

title: Chaplin fidgets bashfully and rubs his chin beside Edna at her typewriter, neither sure what to say
why: Two people, one painfully shy crush, zero words: textbook awkward

title: Rejected, Chaplin sits by the trash cans clutching his flowers and his head slowly droops against the wall
why: The definitive Chaplin comic despair: flowers in hand, next to the garbage

title: Chaplin wakes from a romantic dream to find he is cuddling a mop, recoils in disgust and flings it away
why: The moment reality hits: you were hugging a mop the whole time

title: Close-up of a bulldog sitting at ringside, looking up with a worried, baffled expression
why: A bulldog's furrowed brow says 'what am I watching' better than any human

title: A packed boxing crowd leaps up, waving and roaring with excitement
why: A whole grandstand losing its mind: instant hype cutaway

title: Chaplin wins the fight: his opponent is flat on the canvas as the crowd throws hats into the air
why: The underdog wins and everyone throws their hats: pure victory

title: Harold, high on a skyscraper, lunges and grabs the hands of a giant street clock, legs dangling over the traffic
why: The most famous image in silent comedy, and the perfect 'when the deadline hits' cut.

title: Hanging from the clock, the whole clock face springs open and tips Harold out over the street
why: The thing he is holding onto literally gives way; instant 'and then it got worse'.

title: Clinging to a ledge, Harold gets mobbed by pigeons that flap around his head and knock his hat over his eyes
why: Already in a bad spot, now birds too; reads instantly as 'everything at once'.

title: Close-up: Harold's jaw drops in wide-eyed disbelief, eyes bulging behind his glasses
why: Lloyd's signature wide-eyed 'you want me to do WHAT?' face.

title: Pressed flat against a brick wall high above the street, Harold glances back in terror
why: Pure 'I am not okay' body language, readable at a glance.

title: Close-up: a policeman freezes, eyes popping and mouth agape in astonishment
why: Big theatrical double-take face filling the frame.

title: The same policeman narrows his eyes and slowly strokes his chin with a white glove, sizing someone up
why: Classic 'hmm, I see what you're doing' scheming chin stroke.

title: Harold strolls toward the camera acting innocently casual, whistling, while a glaring cop walks right behind him
why: The universal 'act natural' walk with trouble right on your heels.

title: Close-up: Harold flashes a huge self-satisfied grin straight into the lens
why: Grinning overconfidence is Lloyd's trademark; perfect right after 'how hard can it be?'.

title: Harold stands frozen in a doorway, his face slowly falling as his heart breaks
why: Silent, crushed stare that needs no explanation.

title: Harold throws his arms wide and beams skyward in pure rapture, convinced he has arrived in heaven
why: Over-the-top euphoria, great for 'when the payment finally clears'.

title: Harold's outstretched arms slowly sink as the joy drains from his face into a blank stare
why: The exact moment the hype dies; a perfect reality-check cut.

title: On a girder high above the city, Harold looks down and clutches his head in dizzy panic
why: Instantly says 'I just realised how deep in this I am'.

title: Harold hangs by his hands from a swinging steel girder, face frozen in terror
why: Literally hanging on for dear life; great for 'me clinging to my last brain cell'.

title: Harold and his wife clutch each other in bed, wide-eyed and frozen at a noise in the dark
why: Two terrified faces darting glances: the 'did you hear that?' reaction.

title: After a scolding, Stan and Ollie exchange a look and Ollie dissolves into a giggling, shoulder-shaking laugh
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: Two-shot of the duo trying to keep a straight face and failing: reads as 'we got away with it' instantly.

title: Stan bursts out of the door triumphantly waving the order, then Ollie beams and laughs with delight
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: Pure 'we closed the deal' joy, two quick happy faces, no text.

title: A bulging-eyed James Finlayson peers suspiciously through his door window, mouth agape, then glares sideways
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: A big framed face with saucer eyes peeking out reads as 'who is at my door / I am watching you' in an instant.

title: Stan and Ollie, seated in their car, burst out laughing at their rival
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: Ollie's open-mouthed guffaw is the classic 'laughing at you, not with you' cutaway.

title: James Finlayson turns his head and fixes a slow, seething stare off-screen
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: The master of the slow burn: squinting fury aimed sideways, perfect after an insult.

title: Oliver Hardy sobs theatrically, face screwed up, mopping his tears with a handkerchief
license: Public domain (US film published 1929; per Commons file page)
why: Over-the-top blubbering from a big man is instant comic misery.

title: Stan Laurel slowly turns from a side glance to the camera with narrowed, distrustful eyes
license: Public domain (US film published 1928; per Commons file page)
why: A clean close-up of Stan going from wary glance to a full squint: 'I don't trust this'.

title: Having just wrecked a gumball machine, Ollie looks into the lens with a sheepish, forced smile
license: Public domain (US film published 1928; per Commons file page)
why: Hardy's trademark look to the audience: polite embarrassment that says 'well, that happened'.

title: Count Orlok's huge dark-rimmed eyes rise over the top of a letter and stare unblinking
license: Public domain (1922 film; per Commons file page)
why: Only the eyes over the paper: the creepiest 'I read your message' stare ever filmed; crop keeps the prop letter's scribbles mostly out.

title: A young man freezes mid-meal, staring straight ahead with wide nervous eyes
license: Public domain (1922 film; per Commons file page)
why: Frozen, wide-eyed unease reads as 'I should not have said that' or 'uh oh' with no context.

title: Count Orlok rises stiffly upright from his coffin in the ship's hold, claw hands first
license: Public domain (1922 film; per Commons file page)
why: The iconic rigid rise: the ultimate 'I have returned' / ominous entrance cutaway.

title: A sailor flattens against a beam, arm raised, eyes fixed in pure terror
license: Public domain (1922 film; per Commons file page)
why: Big theatrical silent-film fear; pairs perfectly after the Orlok rise or any scary reveal.

title: A packed 1918 crowd waves hats and flags in wild celebration
license: Public domain (1918 newsreel footage; per Commons file page)
why: A sea of waving hats reads as 'the crowd goes wild'; the crop removes the AP logo bug in the top-right corner.
